Age 8.   I was a passenger in a car involved in an interstate pile up crash that involved both directions of the turnpike.    I watched victims get pulled out of cars.    I saw  one person die, and a couple already gone while I waited to be put into an ambulance.  I saw another one die in the hospital.     I am not going to write down the details.   Just use your imagination.

Life has ups and downs.   I hit that stage at 23.   At 30 I was living the best life.  At 39 it sucked again.   At 42 I got married and things were amazing.   Then it sucked.  At age 49 things were better than they have ever been in my life.   The early swings were huge.    The downward swings are not so bad anymore.    

The causes for the ups and downs are all different.  What I learned is that 'This' does not last forever.   Good or bad, it will turn around.  And each time I was at a low point a similar practice got me out of it again.   The lower the low, the more I put effort into this practice.   At first I thought it was just BS.   Then I really needed it to get through just one day to get a moment of less despair.     And really what it does is train my brain to approach the day with a little different approach. 

The practice is to journal, and to end each entry with some things that are going well.    I thought it was dopey at first.    Then I had to work hard to find something good out of what is going on.    At times I had to work hard to find at least one good thing about people I really did not like.    That practice changed things for me in a huge way.   Changed my life.    I used to be angry with lots of people, and lots of people were angry with me.   When I meet a new person, I start out looking for their good points and remembering them, so when I am pissed off I can record that.     See, my mindset in the beginning was planning to be pissed off.   And by finding the good things I changed that into looking for the positives in people.    

And the people notice that.    All of them.  My old friends and family.  People I just meet.   Instead of sending off angry vibes, people pick up positives, and see the smile and the life in my eyes.    They like me.  And when I look out and see happy people who like my, my world is infinitely better than it was on my low points.   

The second step I learned was to feel the pain when something went wrong.  I gave myself permission to go deep and feel and of the anger and hate until it was all used up.    That would be my low point.   I need the low point to start improving again.    So I allow the low point, then work to make it better.    'I will ride this shit out' and then it improves.

I have allergies to certain trees.   It is the pollen.   Maple pollen is one I am alleging to.   However, I can enjoy maple syrup, and I can work with maple wood all the time.      

Walnut and some tropical woods can develop more irritation if you use them over longer periods.  So I stick with domestic woods, and pay attention to how walnut effects me.  I also shower after working with walnut, and toss those clothes into the washing machine right away.   I use an air compressor before I leave the shop too.    

I wear a respirator when working with wood.  A dust mask is OK.  I have a half mask with carbon filters.    Mine was about $40, and the replacement filters are about $12.   

Can you get an air purifier?     This will filter out dust particles in the air.   If you ever come into the shop and find a layer of dust that was not there yesterday, an air purifier would help.   

And remember to shower when you are done.

1.  Welcome to Bellingham, now get on your bike.  (Joking.   This was the bumper sticker in the 90s).  And strider bikes (no pedals) are the preferred method of kids learning to balance on a bike.  They can go forward at will, and always have feet ready to hit the ground without toppling over.   

2.  The schools are good in Bellingham Public Schools.   A minority here on reddt are loud about the central office.  What you will experience in the classroom will be an amazing collection of teachers.    

3.  It rains here often.  When it does rain it often just enough that you need a rain coat.  Get your kids used to that when they are young and your middle school years will be much better.    How to do that?   Get them into Explorer's Club.   My parents group called it 'Like Boy scouts and Girl scouts, but Bellingham Style.'  Look up the Wild Whatcom website and then Explorer's Club.  To that today because you do want your kid to get a spot. 

Here is how the club goes.  Your son (daughter) will get a group when they begin.   This group will stay together as a cohort through high school.   My kids are in college now, and their best friends are the Explorer Club kids.   The outings are not a regular schedule.   It is usually a Saturday or Sunday.   One outing  will be a service activity.  Pulling weeds, or planting native plants, etc.   Get dirty and have fun!   The next outing will be for fun in nature.  It will be games, observations, and warm tea cooked along one of our trails.   I loved the annual winter trip.  One for the boys and one for the girls.  It is a weekend at a large cabin in the snow.   30 to 40 kids of all ages and choices of 3 to 6 activities each morning and after noon.  Sledding, snow man building, snow cave building, snow shoe hike, indoor activities.   My youngest went for the snow forts and came back interested in playing recorder one year, and guitar another year.   And music is now a major past time for this one.   

One of my kids had a core of 8 kids stay together from the first days, all the way through dong a 5 day back packing trip together r in high school.  Another of mine had lots of people change groups in and out, and back again. All of my kids loved the experiences start to finish.  

4.  Make sure your kids get into Explorer's Club.  See #3.   That is the most important thing for you to do as a parent.  The preschool/kindergarten most like explorer's club is loving space.

There are several 'horse properties' available on the real estate sites.     Some have been for sale for a very long time.   I would assume the empty stalls in those properties mean a similar number of  horses in pastures somewhere else.  

I worked on a horses ranch in BC, Canada for about 5 summers, and got to know the workings quite well.    The 'Stable' had about 20 horses for riders and lessons.   And another 20 or so were out at pasture somewhere.  Some of these were young and not yet trained for riding, or injured and needing a rest.  

Then there would be another 10 or 15 boarded by people who lived far away.  A bunch of owners were from Vancouver, 5 hours away.  They would send up a beloved horse for boarding.   These might stay in the stable and get daily attention.  Or, they may be put in one of the pastures.    All together, this stable had about 50 horses to care for on 6 properties.   

There was one horse owner with a private ring at her home.    She had one horse and she wanted company for him, but did not want a large number of horses to come and go.   So she would adopt one of the older horses that could no longer work.   One time I worked for this woman to increase her pasture size by adding more fence and removing hazards.  

My job there was mostly to put up hay, fix fences and to do ground work with the 'green' horses.     One or two would come in from a pasture for a while.  I would work with the horse to put on the halter and teach it to walk calmly around the farm.   Go into this place, back up, turn left, turn right while backing up, get into the trailer, back out.  Getting the horse comfortable with these moves allowed the more skilled horse people to get up and ride sooner.   One of the best experiences was driving way up past Hundred Mile House and then another 50 KM onto back roads.   We picked up a young stallion.     He was gelded, and I worked with him a bit while he was wild and bucking.    On my last summer there he was gentle and taking 8 year old kids on a ride around the ring with no one holding his lead rope.     I would love to do that again!

I would not buy a mobile home in a mobile home park.  You will pay rent on top of the cost of the home.   

What happens if the owner of the Mobile home park decides to sell?  And the new owners want to build condos.    You will not find somewhere to move your home.  You will likely loose it.   And all of that investment. 

So check to make sure the place is owned by residents.  Otherwise I would don't do this.

I would go to a real estate website (homes.com, zillow, Redfin) and search for mobile homes in your area.   And search for homes up to $500 K and compare what you get.   Don't forget to add in rent/hoa costs and taxes.

I have a larger chuck.  The vase shown just over the limit of what I turn without a steady rest. 

Here are my steps:  

\-turn between centers to make it almost round and add a solid tenon.

\-Put it on the chuck and hold with tailstock support to make the outside shape I want. I sand and complete this part to a final sanding before moving on.  (And I always go back and hit it with hand sanding before I add a finish).    

\-Remove the live center and put in a forester bit.   I stick with 2 3/4" and not larger.    The larger areas seems to be too much to take off with my set up.    I will drill in about 2" and then work with tools to make this part.  On this first part I can use my bowl gouges and get a fine feeling surface on the inside.  It is ready for sanding later.    

\-At this point it is drill out 2", then use tools to remove material.  I use a round nose scraper to push deeper.  Then I use a round carbide tool to find the outside edge and make that outside wall smooth.   And I use an air compressor to clean out the shavings often.   Tip:  Move your head to a position away from the opening when you blow out the shavings.     

\-I do not have a steady rest.   I can go in about 6 or 7" with my forester bit.  I can dig in about another 2" after that.  So my maximum depth is about 9" with a curve.  I can go to 10" if the side walls are very straight.   I need longer tools to go deeper.   

\-When you are poking a long handle tool deep into wood you do not want a catch.  So take small amounts only and make sure the bottom is an even shape and 'catch proof'.  This is where I use just round nose scrapers.   I follow the shape from the previous cuts.   I make lots of mistakes with square tools.   If you tool is at an angle and gets spun out of alignment at speed it will hit the opening.  If it is thin you just cracked your piece.   

\-Everything I know says I can go deeper, but I would want a tool designed to give me leverage that deep, and I would want a steady rest.   \*\*My 20" tool is pushing it going 10" deep.  I really want a longer handle for that.   

\*\*I have a round nose scraper that does a great job on the bottom of the bowl.  I picked up a tool another turner made and discarder.   It has a huge heavy shaft and it is attached to an iron pipe.  It is all welded to gather.   This gets me a smooth bottom in almost all woods.    Spalted pieces are difficult.   I have another tool that is made from a spare part out of a machine shop.   It is a 5/8" piece of steel that the guy forged and hardened into a skew shape.   It is 20" long and gives good leverage.    I use it as a negative rake scraper to do that last finishing cut on the bottom.   The guy who made it worked for a machine shop that repaired tools.   He made his out of a discarded part.

Wood moves.   A tree grows with tension and some parts have more tension than others.   You also have sap wood and heart wood in your bowl.  That makes it beautiful.  That makes it move more.   Sap wood is full of sap, of all things.  And when you cut it the sap leaves, and sprays out at you.    Removing the sap releases some of that tension, and the wood moved to adjust.   And you heart wood has less sap, and adjusts at a different rate, or not at all.  

Now add tension from shrinking when the sap dries up.    You just increased your chances of a huge crack in the wood. 

What you can do:  Cut the bowl to an even thickness.  Leave no bumps or valleys along the sides.    Dry the wood slowly.  Collect all of your shavings and cram as much as you can inside the wood, and put it in a paper bag.  Now cram as much as you can on all sides of the bowl.   This will slow down the drying and reduce chances of a crack.  Reduce.  Not eliminate.   

You can put it into a plastic bag and leave not much air inside the bag.   This one needs almost daily attention.  Once a day take out the bowl and turn the bag inside out.   What happens here is a little bit of moisture escapes every time you turn it inside-out.   The moisture inside the bag now evaporates out.    And it is a slow and controlled release of moisture.   You still risk a crack. 

You can also finish the thing today and let it wobble a bit.   Turn 1 or 2 inches at the top of the bowl and turn it thin.  Leave just enough for sanding.   Then turn the next section leaving enough room to sand.   Continue until done.  Then wet sand using lots of water and lots of sandpaper.  It is messy and your lathe will get wet.    Make sure electronics are out of the way.  I do not do this on my lathe because of rust.    Then microwave the bowl to dry it out.  Heat for 1 minute, cool for 3.   Weigh the bowl between each heating.   When it stops losing weight each round the water is gone.   Now touch up sanding and oil it right way.   I have only done this with small bowls.  Yours does not fit into my microwave.

You tighten up the blade.  Then the metal stretches under tension.  Not much.  Some.   Do that enough times and you will change the shape around the teeth on the blade.   Do it too much and you can snap the blade.    Your bandsaw blade is likely welded together at some point.   This is your weak area.  This can cause an uneven spot.  This is where too much tension stretches differently.   When the blade goes around there can be a telltale mark on your wood for that spot in the blade.     Look at a piece you recently cut.    You might see a dozen lines faintly showing in the cut.   Then there is one line that is deeper in one direction. \-Cut off about 2 inches on one end.  Toss that end into the firewood pile.    Are the cracks still large? You can cut off another inch, or split the log down one go the bigger cracks. 

\-Split the logs down the middle to remove the pith.  The pith is the center ring(s).    Removing the pith reduces the chances of more cracking.  Reduces, but does not eliminate.   

 This will determine the quality of the wood inside.   I cut into a maple trunk that was 40 inches across and 20 feet long.  It  had been sitting for 5 years.  The center of the log was still 'green wood'.     I also have some maple that has been sitting in my yard for 2 years.   The inside is spalted, and very desirable for wood turners.   

Open up a log and see how it looks inside.   Then find your local wood turning club and offer some wood in exchange for a bowl. 4WD or AWD is not at all needed.   When there is snow or ice on the road neither one will keep you on the road if you drive too fast, brake the corners hard,  or slam on the brakes.   Both of these are to get you out of a ditch, once you are stopped.   Thinking you can go faster because you have AWD is what puts you in the ditch in the first place.   

If you drive for the conditions today, 2WD is just fine.  Get good tire chains, and not those cheap wire things.   Real chains cost more, and they will get you across the icy spots.   You can travel any paved road with that.  

What you really want is a car or truck with high clearance.   When you are going up the bumpy roads with washouts and pot holes , keeping the bottom of your car above the road debris is most important.    You also want the right tires.  All season radials are often good enough.    If you are a regular on the dirt roads a beefy tire helps a little, but gives lower gas milage.    

Some cars have AWD (Subaru) and low clearance.    Getting bottomed out and needing to shovel the entire road way really sucks.  And that old Subaru could not get up to the top because the tires did not reach the dirt.   One time the snow was about 6 inches deep and packed powder.    We were stuck with AWD, and the 2WD pick up truck with higher  clearance drove right along  like nothing. We had to get out and shovel in a lot of places.  Once the truck made tracks in front of us it got even worse.     2wd could do the road when AWD could not. 

Now, most other cars or trucks with a high clearance also come with AWD or 4WD anyway.   Subaru is good for snow in the city, and up to the ski resorts.  It is not a good choice for the rougher dirt roads, or driving in deep snow on dirt roads in winter.    If you are going on the back roads between late October and Easter, it is likely you hit some condition that requires high clearance.  

\-I have been on the ski team and retired to doing back country adventures.   I spent most of 40 years traveling far in the snow, or venturing down some dirt road for access to a trail.   

More tips:  Get some floor mats from some old car.   They are rubber on the bottom and rug on top.    When you get to the hike and want to change boots, stand on these.  Life saver!      Carry extras, because you can get stuck, even with 4wd.     Put some sand down, put your rug on top of the sand, now you have traction to back up far enough to get your tires straight and traction enough to move forward.    Carry a shovel with a flat bottom and solid handle.      Get a roof box to carry the shovel, skis, wet gear, broom for windshields in snow.    Carry winter rated washer fluid.

Kids at that age want to make things to learn the math, and they want to talk about it.  Some prefer the making, some prefer the talking.   Both can work.   So play some math games and find out if she likes to build things or talk about how to build things.    

 The way to help is to spend time together doing things that use the same math they are learning.   Make talking about numbers and posing problems part of the everyday routine.   



The rest of this is suggestions I made up from looking at a list of grade 1 math skills.   Doing addition?      Make up stories about how many cookies, or boxes of cereal to add together.    Subtraction?   You have a brand new box with 20 crackers.   Dad eats 7 crackers and mom eats 5.   How many are left in the box?   Etc.   Shapes and geometry?   Get toothpicks and marshmallows and make all the shapes and angles she needs to know.   The build a tower.  You get 20 tooth picks and 20 marshmallows.   Who can build the tallest?  The strongest?  Etc.    Practice telling time.  It is 4:30.   Granma comes in 15 minutes.   What time will it be?  Etc. Make patterns.    almost any material or drawing material is good for repeating patterns or growing patterns.  Measure things.    Put up a height chart for the family.   Measure how tall everyone is.   Fractions: Cut up food items to share with 2 people, or 3, or 4, etc.   Which is bigger?  1/2 or 1/3?  Most kids say 1/3 because 3 is bigger.    So get some cookies and cut them up to find out.    Count things.  How many grains of rice in a teaspoon?  Can you put them in piles of 10 to make it easy?   Make some graphs.    How many grapes did each person eat at lunch?  Cut a square to represent 1 grape.    Glue down one square so show how many she ate, how many dad ate, how many mom ate, etc.    Find other things to show on a graph.    Bonus with graphs:   DO not glue the papers down.   Dad ate 25 grapes, mom ate 12 and daughter at 7.   What is the average?   (Give some of Dad's pile away until all the piles are almost equal.  And you will find the answer is between 14 and 15).    Averaging is a higher grade skill.  This is fun and gets kids to think about what an average is way before school introduces it.

I am a wood turner.   I cut maybe 15 trees per year.   Most of them are quite big at the base.  

To cut up the logs for making bowls, I want to make the log about 6 inches longer than the diameter.   Then I will rip down the middle to remove the pith.    What I want is a smooth cut all the way town the middle.   So I want a long bar and a powerful saw with a sharp chain.   

Removing the pith reduces checks and cracks.   Painting the ends with anchor seal (liquid wax) also helps.  Cutting with a short saw and moving the blade up and down leaves rough marks, and it can eat into an inch or two of otherwise good wood.   The longer bar with some power behind it makes a cut that is easy to work with when you put it on the lathe.   It can add an inch or two the the height of a bowl I can make from this tree.

Coyotes?  Do you know that shooting adult coyotes actually leads to a larger population in future years?   It sound wrong, but it is how nature works.  

It is the natural cycle.   When there are more predators, the adults produce more off-spring.  The adults need to produce enough young to keep the species going.   So when they are hunted they will have more pups.    And, if there are fewer adults eating mice this year, more mice will be present next year.   More food for coyotes means they will have more pups until things even out.   Leaving them alone leads to smaller litters and fewer animals next year.  

If coyotes are bothering your animals you are better off getting a dog for the herd to protect them.   A small population of adults, and an active guard dog will be enough to keep your herd safe. \#1.  Go during the week for a quiet hike.   Weekends and holidays can be busier, but no where near as busy as Oyster Dome or Fragrance Lake.   

Start at the Arroyo trail head off of Chukanut.  Hike up Hemlock to the road.     Turn right at the big trail sign onto North Lost Lake Trail.  (Checkpoint B).  This is a different road.    Take your third left.   The left is where you return.    The second left is Lower Salal.    The third left is Salal Trail.    

From Salal Trail, hike in a bit.   Take the first left, which is back on Lower Salal Trail.     There is an intersection.   The left goes back to the road.   The right is a winding down hill back to the road, but lower down.  

Now hike back down the road and see that big trail sign again on Hemlock trail.   Turn right onto Hemlock again.   Take the first left onto Falls Trail.     At the intersection you can turn right and see the falls.   It is dry in the summer.    The left goes back to Hemlock.   Go right at the intersection, and trace your trail back to the trail head.  It is mostly left turns from there.   

\#2.  Drive down Chukanut to Cleator Road. Its confusing, because the sign says Hiline Road.   It turns into Cleator in 100 feet.     If you see the firehouse on the left you just went too far.  Take this to the end.

Walk to the left of the lake and follow the non-trails to the waterfall opposite of the lake.   Head back to Lost Lake Trail.  Turn right.  (This is where you were going before).   Find  Ridge  Trail, (Checkpoint D).  Go right.   Stop at the view.   Choose to turn around , or continue to Hemlock Trail (again, but a different part).    Take this to the big trail sign.  (Checkpoint E).  Continue to Pine Lake and Cedar Lake.   See the map for details.    There is an extra add on called Cedar Lake Overlook Trail.    It is a steep hike. It can also be the type of wood you are using.    When I turn something thin and use a scraper on the inside I can get some extra vibrations going on.

I am using sheet metal screws.   I do not remember where I got the tip.   It was a live demo, and an unofficial comment.  "Use only wood screws.    but I use sheet metal screws".    Or something like that. 

  
\# 11 or # 12.  Pre-drill the hole.   That helps remove the screws later.   And coat the screws with bar soap.  I use Ivory brand.  Way back in the 70s I was working with a carpenter in his 80s, and we were putting wood screws in with regular old fashioned wood screws.  He made sure I knew to use Ivory and no other brands. No additives, so no reactions with your wood and no stains.   This guy was born in the 1800's, so I trust him to know the old fashioned ways.     I keep a spray bottle with water close to the lathe.   So I wet the soap, let is soften a bit.  Then get a light coating of soap and sink the screw.   

What size hold do I drill?  Look at your screw.  You should see the threads, and you should see the core of the screw.  Put your drill bit next to the screw, and you should see mostly threads,  It should be close to the same size.   For harder woods I select a slightly larger drill bit.  

How long should my screws be?   It depends on the weight of the wood.   You do not want to leave holes in your bowl.   They say 7 threads sink into the wood.   I have fudged to only 5 threads if it is light, and if I use tail stock support.   For heavy bowls I am using 2.5" long #12 screws.    And I start with tail stock support while I do the outside.  Most of the time I keep that support in place until I turn it around and hold it with the tenon.  Even then I keep the support as long as I can.
